title: Choosing a Self-Hosted Service Desk: A Practitioner’s Decision Guide
summary:
A self-hosted service desk is more than a ticketing application installed on your own infrastructure. Requests still need to move from intake through assignment, escalation, resolution, and useful knowledge capture—and the team operating the system needs to be able to maintain it.

This guide compares nine options by deployment fit, service-management depth, asset and knowledge support, licensing, and day-to-day administration. Verify the specific edition and version before treating a product as self-hosted. If AI is part of your requirements, confirm whether it works within your private environment and can connect to an enterprise-managed model.

Comparison table

  • Deployment fit: Verify the edition and version, infrastructure requirements, and support for restricted or air-gapped environments if needed.
  • Service workflow depth: Trace a request from intake to assignment, workflow decisions, updates, resolution, and knowledge capture. A ticket list may not cover processes that cross teams or require approvals.
  • Asset tracking: Check whether technicians can use asset records as part of service work, rather than treating inventory as a separate system or checklist item.
  • Operating and licensing fit: Include setup, administration, support, and licensing prerequisites in the comparison.   2. ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus: Compare the self-hosted edition and its ticketing, request, knowledge, and asset workflows with your requirements.
  3. BMC Helix ITSM: Evaluate for complex ITIL-oriented processes, while accounting for implementation effort.
  4. Ivanti Neurons for ITSM: Consider configurable service workflows, but verify the deployment configuration and asset scope.
  5. TOPdesk: Compare request, knowledge, and service processes, and confirm the edition and administration requirements.
  6. GLPI: Evaluate when open-source ITSM and asset inventory matter together; plan for self-hosting and administration.
  7. Znuny: Assess its self-hosted ticket workflow against internal service processes and maintenance capacity.
  8. osTicket: Consider for focused self-hosted support-ticket handling; it is not a substitute for a broad ITSM suite.

Detailed reviews

ONES.com

Product Overview

ONES.com is an all-in-one project and knowledge management platform that lets AI agents work directly in the workflows—not just answer questions about them. For service management with self-hosted deployment, it combines privately deployed work management with ONES Desk, a ticket-management add-on for handling customer requests. ONES On-Premises is deployed within your organization’s infrastructure and supports single-node, cluster, high-availability, and air-gapped deployments (deployment details).

Why It Was Selected

ONES.com stands out for teams that need both customer ticket handling and control over where their service-management environment runs. With ONES Desk, a customer submits a ticket through the portal; the submission creates an issue in the project, where a service representative can update its status, respond, or assign it to another person. That gives the team a concrete path from intake to ownership and response, rather than a portal disconnected from the work used to manage the request (ONES Desk ticket workflow).

The fit also depends on service-desk scope and team size. ONES Desk is sold as an add-on with ONES Project, costs $42 per named user annually for 1–500 users, and is available on-premises; the on-premises subscription has a 100-user minimum (ONES Desk pricing; ONES On-Premises pricing). These terms make the package and minimum commitment visible when you compare operational needs with licensing and administration resources.

Core Capabilities

  • Pain: A customer request arrives without a clear work record. Capability: A portal submission creates an issue that a service representative can process. Result: The request has a trackable work item for follow-up.
  • Pain: The customer needs an update after submitting a ticket. Capability: The representative can change ticket status and respond to the customer. Result: The service interaction progresses through an explicit status and reply.
  • Pain: A request needs attention from someone outside the initial handler. Capability: The representative can assign the ticket to other personnel. Result: Ownership can move to the person responsible for the next action.
  • Pain: Support staff need to manage incoming work as a queue of active records. Capability: Tickets are handled as project issues that representatives can process and update. Result: The team works from service records rather than relying only on the original submission.
  • Pain: A service team must keep its environment within its own infrastructure. Capability: ONES On-Premises supports customer-infrastructure deployment, including single-node, cluster, high-availability, and air-gapped options. Result: The organization can select a deployment configuration aligned with its infrastructure requirements.
  • Pain: Deployment planning must account for scale and operating resources. Capability: The on-premises subscription has a 100-user minimum. Result: The minimum commitment is clear during team-size and budget planning.
  • Pain: Ticket-management costs need to be assessed alongside the underlying platform. Capability: ONES Desk is a named-user add-on purchased with ONES Project, with an annual rate for 1–500 users. Result: Buyers can account for both the service-desk add-on and its required platform purchase.

Pros

  • Customer-infrastructure deployment includes options from single-node to air-gapped configurations.
  • Ticket intake creates project issues that representatives can update, answer, and assign, connecting request handling with accountable work.
  • Published Desk pricing and the on-premises user minimum provide concrete inputs for licensing and scale assessment.

Cons

  • ONES Desk must be purchased with ONES Project, so licensing requires evaluating the combined package.
  • The on-premises subscription has a 100-user minimum, which is a material commitment to include in budget and rollout planning.
  • Escalation is managed through custom workflows, fields, and automation rather than a built-in escalation feature (ONES Desk escalation guidance).

Pricing

ONES On-Premises provides a 30-day free trial for up to 20 users. Paid plans use annual tiered per-seat pricing, with a 100-user minimum. See ONES.com Pricing.

Best For

ONES.com is best for organizations seeking self-hosted ticket handling where customer submissions need to become assigned, updateable work records, and where the team can plan around the on-premises minimum and paired Desk-and-Project licensing. For example, a service representative can receive a portal request, update its status, reply to the customer, and assign follow-up work while the service environment runs within the organization’s infrastructure. That combination makes it a strong option when deployment control and a connected intake-to-response workflow are the deciding requirements.

ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus

ServiceDesk Plus is an IT service-management and help-desk platform with self-hosted and cloud editions. Assess its incident and request handling, workflow configuration, knowledge functions, and ITIL-oriented processes against a representative request—for example, an access request that must pass through approval.

Trade-offs: Available functions depend on edition and version, so confirm the precise self-hosted offering. Implementation, licensing, administration, and support can require more planning than a basic ticketing setup. Pricing depends on the edition and licensing arrangement; confirm the current terms.

Best fit: IT teams seeking structured request and incident workflows that can support the required service processes, and able to evaluate and operate the chosen edition.

BMC Helix ITSM

BMC Helix ITSM is aimed at enterprise service management and complex IT operations. Evaluate how its request handling, workflows, knowledge practices, and ITIL-oriented processes map to your actual work, including approvals and fulfillment. Treat asset inventory and tracking as separate requirements to verify in the selected configuration.

Trade-offs: Enterprise implementation and licensing can be a substantial commitment. Self-hosted suitability depends on the particular edition and version, so verify deployment, implementation, and support requirements before shortlisting.

Best fit: Organizations with complex service processes, the resources for an enterprise implementation, and requirements that map to the confirmed configuration.

Ivanti Neurons for ITSM

Ivanti Neurons for ITSM is a service-management option to assess for incident and request workflows, knowledge management, and ITIL-oriented practices. Map a real issue—from recording and assignment through resolution—to the edition and deployment you intend to operate. Check whether asset inventory and tracking are included in that configuration.

Trade-offs: Self-hosted availability varies by product configuration and must be confirmed. Licensing, implementation, ongoing administration, asset scope, and support arrangements also need to be checked against available staff and budget.

Best fit: Teams that need structured service workflows and can validate deployment and capability fit for the specific configuration they plan to use.

TOPdesk

TOPdesk provides structured service management for incidents, requests, knowledge, and broader processes such as changes and problems. Its hosted and self-hosted options should be evaluated separately: confirm that the chosen edition can run on your infrastructure, then map its workflows to your service practices.

Trade-offs: A self-hosted installation adds infrastructure and ongoing administration responsibilities. Confirm coverage for the specific ITIL processes you need; pricing depends on the selected arrangement and is not stated here as a fixed public amount.

Best fit: Service teams seeking defined request and service processes that can operate and administer their own deployment.

GLPI

GLPI combines IT service management with asset inventory and tracking. That can keep equipment context close to a support request—for example, when a technician investigates a reported laptop problem. Its open-source option supports self-hosting.

Trade-offs: Open-source software still requires internal capacity to deploy, administer, and maintain. Teams should compare its service-management depth with complex ITIL needs and confirm the support or paid-service arrangement that fits their operations.

Best fit: Organizations that want service requests and asset records in the same operational tool and have the capacity to run it.

Znuny

Znuny is an open-source, self-hosted service desk centered on ticket handling. Staff can capture requests, track progress, and manage responses in a shared queue; technical teams can assess the platform against their own processes and configuration needs.

Trade-offs: Self-hosting places installation, upgrades, security, backups, and administration on your organization. Assess asset inventory, knowledge management, and ITIL process coverage separately rather than assuming a ticket workflow supplies them.

Best fit: Technically capable teams prioritizing self-hosted ticket management and able to maintain the system.

osTicket

osTicket is an open-source help desk that can be self-hosted. Email and web forms can collect requests; agents can organize tickets into queues, assign them, add internal notes, communicate with requesters, and track status. Configurable forms can capture details such as request type or affected device.

Trade-offs: Its focus is support ticketing, not a complete asset inventory or broad ITIL suite. Complex approvals, reporting, or asset lifecycle requirements may need customization or additional systems. The organization is responsible for maintaining a self-hosted installation.

Best fit: Small support teams that need clear request-to-resolution tracking and have the technical capacity to operate the help desk.

SolarWinds Web Help Desk

SolarWinds Web Help Desk combines help-desk ticketing with asset tracking, knowledge management, and reporting. Asset records can provide context while technicians handle a support request, while knowledge and reporting support repeatable answers and operational review.

Trade-offs: It is oriented toward IT help-desk operations, so compare its process depth with broader service-management or complex ITIL requirements. Confirm the current self-hosted edition and plan for infrastructure and administration. Pricing depends on the applicable licensing arrangement.

Best fit: IT teams that need ticket handling and asset tracking together and can operate the required deployment.

  1. Set the deployment boundary. Record the required infrastructure, edition, and any restricted-network or air-gap constraints. Remove products that cannot meet them.
  2. Walk through a real request. Trace intake, assignment, workflow decisions, updates, knowledge use, asset context, and resolution. Compare the actual steps rather than counting features.
  3. Check operating fit. Include licensing prerequisites, implementation, administration, and support. For ONES.com, account for Desk requiring ONES Project, the $42 annual Desk rate per named user for 1–500 users, and the 100-user on-premises minimum. See Desk pricing and on-premises terms.

Conclusion

ONES.com is worth shortlisting when you need self-hosted portal requests to become work records representatives can process, update, answer, or assign—and your team can meet the 100-user on-premises minimum and paired Desk-and-Project licensing requirements. GLPI is a relevant alternative when open-source ITSM and asset inventory are central. For complex ITIL-oriented processes, evaluate BMC Helix ITSM against your process scope and implementation capacity. For every finalist, verify the exact self-hosted edition and test the same representative request and asset scenario before deciding.

title: Simplified Chinese in Traditional Chinese app translations: 1 in 4 apps ship it
summary:
Chinese Android apps usually ship two translations: Simplified (values-zh-rCN) for mainland China and Singapore, and Traditional (values-zh-rTW, values-zh-rHK) for Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau. Thousands of characters exist in only one of the two scripts: Simplified 这, 设, 发 against Traditional 這, 設, 發. A Simplified-only character in a Traditional file is text that was never converted, or only partly converted, and users in Taipei or Hong Kong see it.

I pre-registered four predictions about this before reading any app, then counted across 4,693 F-Droid source repositories. The character sets came from OpenCC's dictionaries (3,771 Simplified-only and 3,198 Traditional-only characters).

Prediction Result Verdict
P1: at least 10% of apps with a Traditional translation ship a Simplified-only character in it 188 of 692 apps (27.2%) held
P2: in the typical app with a flag, at least half the flagged strings are copies of the app's own Simplified string mean 0.39 over 183 apps failed
P3: the reverse leak (Traditional characters in Simplified files) is rarer 0.18% vs 0.87% of strings held
P4: apps with no Simplified file to copy from leak less 0.08% vs 0.88% of strings held

Copies dominate the count, not the apps. 67% of flagged strings are character-for-character copies of the app's Simplified string, but five apps hold 54% of all flagged strings, where large parts of a Taiwan or Hong Kong file are in Simplified. In the typical app with a flag, the leak is one or two characters left in otherwise converted text: 内 for 內, 来 for 來, 对 for 對. The prediction was weighted by app on purpose, so it failed.

Apps with nothing to copy from almost never leak. Of 42 apps whose only Chinese translation is Traditional, 3 ship a flag (4 strings in total).

The check is precise. A hand check (not pre-registered) of 40 flagged strings found 39 real defects. The one false alarm is Cantonese: Hong Kong writers use 晒 for the particle meaning "all", while OpenCC treats it as the Simplified form of 曬. Only 3 of 2,721 flagged strings name "简体中文" on purpose in a language picker.

It also held on text it was not tuned on. A second pre-registered test ran the same detector on the same apps' store listings (F-Droid and Google Play descriptions and release notes). Of 35 flagged listing lines drawn before anyone read them, 32 were real defects (the prediction was at least 80%). Fewer apps leak there than I predicted: 25 of 287 apps with a Traditional listing (8.7%, below my 10%), and one app holds 216 of the 295 flagged lines. Apps whose string files leak are more likely to leak in their listings too: 8 of 48 against 11 of 172.

Limits. This is a lower bound: Simplified text written with characters both scripts share isn't counted, and neither is mainland vocabulary in Traditional characters (軟件 for 軟體). It is one snapshot of default branches on 1 and 2 November 2026, and the hand checks were done by AI agents, not native readers.

If you maintain an app with a Taiwan or Hong Kong translation, a quick check is to search those files for a few common Simplified-only characters such as 这, 设, 发, 说, 个 and 们.

Results, code and every flagged string: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/android-translation-crash-census/blob/main/hanzi-leak/RESULTS.md

The pre-registration, published before the run: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/android-translation-crash-census/blob/main/hanzi-leak/PREREG.md

The store-listing test, with every hand label: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/android-translation-crash-census/blob/main/hanzi-meta/RESULTS.md

An earlier study with the same design, Russian letters in Ukrainian and Belarusian translations: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/android-translation-crash-census/blob/main/cyrillic-leak/RESULTS.md

This study and post were made with AI agents.

MV2, Munim, Inc.

title: Building Adaptive Activity Goals in a Privacy-First React Native Fitness App
summary:
I've reached another milestone in EdgeFit, my open-source, privacy-first fitness companion built with React Native, TypeScript, HealthKit, and SQLite.

The latest feature is Adaptive Activity Goals.

This feature builds on two earlier milestones:

  1. A 30-Day Activity Calendar to visualize historical activity.
  2. Personal Activity Insights to explain trends and consistency.

Now EdgeFit can use that history to suggest personalized daily step goals.

Why adaptive goals?

Many fitness applications use a fixed daily step target.

But a single target doesn't reflect everyone's activity patterns, routines, or starting point.

I wanted to explore a different approach: suggest goals based on the user's own recent activity rather than assuming everyone should aim for the same number.

The challenge isn't simply calculating an average. It's deciding when a recommendation is supported by enough data, how quickly a goal should change, and how to keep users in control.

The approach: Explainable rules first

For this phase, I chose deterministic recommendations instead of introducing machine learning.

The design focuses on several principles.

1. Use recent activity history

Recent step data provides a starting point for a personalized recommendation.

A goal can be informed by a person's recorded activity rather than an arbitrary universal target.

2. Account for missing data

Missing HealthKit data should not automatically be treated as zero steps.

Otherwise, incomplete history could produce an artificially low recommendation.

Data coverage matters as much as the calculation itself.

3. Avoid sudden changes

A single unusually active day shouldn't necessarily result in a substantially higher daily goal.

Recommendations should reflect meaningful activity patterns rather than isolated spikes.

4. Explain the recommendation

Users should be able to understand why a goal was suggested.

This is one reason deterministic rules are valuable: the inputs and decision logic can be inspected and tested.

5. Preserve user control

A recommendation should remain a recommendation.

Users need the ability to decide which goals work for them instead of being forced to follow an algorithm.

Keeping the architecture privacy-first

EdgeFit uses HealthKit for activity data and SQLite for local persistence.

Adaptive Activity Goals extends this local-first approach, rather than introducing a cloud-based recommendation service.

The aim is to make personal health data useful without making remote processing a prerequisite.

Why not use machine learning yet?

I'm interested in on-device AI, but I don't want to add ML simply to label a feature intelligent.

First, I want a reliable rule-based baseline.

Then I can experiment with a lightweight on-device model and evaluate:

  • Does it produce more useful recommendations?
  • Is the improvement measurable?
  • How much latency does inference introduce?
  • What is the memory and energy cost?
  • Can the recommendation still be explained?

If a deterministic algorithm works just as well, that's a useful engineering finding too.

What's next?

My next goal is to investigate on-device machine learning for activity pwersonalization.

EdgeFit is open source, and feedback is welcome.

GitHub: https://github.com/raviseta/edgefit

If you're building health, fitness, or privacy-first mobile applications, I'd love to hear how you approach adaptive recommendations and incomplete sensor data.

title: Open Source Radar · 2026-11-02: Agent infrastructure is splitting into replaceable parts
summary:
By Renchao Wu. Originally published on widechaos.cn.

For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-02.

All five point at the same thing: infrastructure for agents; retrieval, a knowledge base, a skills directory, an evolution loop, and one course that turns evaluation into a specification.

1. sahenjp/RustXNG ⭐ 471 · Rust

GitHub: https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG

In one line: A self-hosted search service that returns ranked results and page text in a single request, built to be an agent's retrieval layer.

What it is: Written in Rust, AGPL-3.0-or-later, a port of SearXNG with a SearXNG-compatible response shape and a browser UI on port 8888. The repository was created on 18 October 2026 and reached v0.26.0 in two weeks, with two releases on 1 November.

What stands out:

  • Text comes back with the results. With include_raw_content=1 it returns about 32,000 characters from the top five pages, so an agent can inspect extracted text without fetching every page separately. Extraction does not establish source accuracy, completeness or permission to republish it.
  • Several upstream engines with per-engine failure handling. 226 engine types, 352 settings entries, 180 enabled by default; each engine has its own timeout, failed engines are suspended with backoff, and engines that keep returning nothing are rested.
  • The project documents default SSRF checks. The documented policy restricts fetching to public addresses. I have not tested redirects, DNS changes or the full network boundary; it is not an independent security guarantee.
  • Ops surface included. /healthz, OpenMetrics /metrics, response cache, image proxy, bot rate limiting, and idle timeout for sidecars.

Compared with: The relationship to SearXNG is a port, not a fork in spirit; compatible interface, engines carried over, plus page-text fetching, SSRF protection and a ranking pass (term coverage, site authority, identifier match). Those additions are documented by the project; I did not re-check them against SearXNG item by item. Against hosted search APIs the difference is self-hosting and text volume: the README reports a 100-question comparison on one machine, hit@1 of 79–83 versus Exa 77 and Tavily 34; about 32,000 characters per request versus about 9,000 and about 1,200; 0.01 s for a repeated query versus 0.6 s and about 1 s. Those are the project's own numbers, not my tests, and it notes they move a few points between runs.

Recent updates: v0.26.0 (1 November) published a ghcr.io image and made the English README primary; v0.25.0 the same day repositioned the project as an agent retrieval layer. All three release notes are one line about checksums, so the substance is in the commit messages.

Who it's for: Anyone who wants to host an agent-search endpoint. The metasearch service still sends queries to enabled upstream engines and fetches third-party pages; self-hosting does not make retrieval offline or eliminate third-party data exposure. Two conditions apply: Google is unavailable in this build (the WML endpoint returns 403, the HTML endpoint needs JavaScript, headless browsers get detected), so replacement engines need testing; and the license is AGPL-3.0-or-later, whose exact terms should be checked for the intended deployment. The README specifically discusses source obligations for a modified network-service version; network access alone is not a complete licence analysis.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Collapsing "found it" and "got citable text" into one request is the right subtraction; whether it replaces an existing setup depends on results without Google.

Checked: README, three release notes, recent commits and docs/COMPARISON-EXA.md; not installed.

2. undefined-ui/second-brain-os ⭐ 1,170 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/undefined-ui/second-brain-os

In one line: A plain-Markdown knowledge base an agent maintains for you, plus a course and toolkit for building that agent.

What it is: 130 pages; a guide, a seven-module agents course and five handbooks; with a toolkit of 18 skills, 72 slash commands, 6 subagents, 4 scripts, a plugin and a starter vault. MIT. Obsidian is a viewer, not a dependency. It implements the llm-wiki pattern Karpathy published as a gist on 4 April 2026: the wiki is primary and raw sources are an archive; new sources get compiled into existing pages; three operations; ingest, lint, query.

What stands out:

  • Compilation, not side-by-side summaries. A concept page is rewritten and thickened by new sources instead of becoming a list of excerpts. That is a maintenance choice; I have not measured long-term accuracy or upkeep.
  • Maintenance is a command, not a reminder. 72 slash commands cover creating pages, merging, health checks and graph export; /metrics, /health and /graph-export run from scripts inside the vault.
  • Health has script-generated indicators. The health and graph-export entry points provide observable indicators. A health score or graph export does not by itself detect every contradiction or establish that stored claims are true.
  • The resource list is dated. Every entry in resources/ carries one line on why it belongs, and the README states it was checked on 1 November 2026 with stars from that day's API.

Compared with: The README compares this file-maintenance approach with memory servers and retrieval-based context assembly. This one is a methodology document plus a copyable vault plus a command set, and its bet is that an agent maintains files through fixed operations. It names Basic Memory 1.0, ai-memory 3.0 and Hindsight 1.0 and explains how it differs; that is its own account, and I did not read those repositories. The checkable dimensions are three: whether writes leave evidence, whether pages are compiled, and whether lint actually runs.

Recent updates: No releases; main-branch iteration. On 2 November the graph recommendation moved from Kuzu to Ladybug (Kuzu was archived in October 2025; the project describes Ladybug as a continuation with embedded CSV support; I have not independently verified migration compatibility), and the README was reorganised by level with a "new this month" section. A companion site went up on 14 October.

Who it's for: People already keeping file-based notes who want an agent to take over filing and linking. It assumes Claude Code's directory conventions (.claude/skills, commands, agents); another agent means changing how they load. If you want "install it and it organises itself", this is not that; it gives process and scripts, and you still feed it the first ten sources.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. The method matters more than the tooling, and here the method is written as executable commands.

Checked: README, the llm-wiki pattern document and recent commits; not installed.

3. ant-research/AntOmniEvo ⭐ 1,221 · Python

GitHub: https://github.com/ant-research/AntOmniEvo

In one line: A framework that treats a system's tunable parts as a directory of files, has a coding agent rewrite them from failure trajectories, and keeps the loop and the audit trail.

What it is: Python, Apache-2.0. The division of labour is "you define, the framework controls, AI does the work": you supply how to run the system, an evaluator, train/val data, a directory mapping for the tunable artifacts, and a starting point; the framework handles scheduling, budgets, selection and persistence; a coding agent acts as the Proposer. Tunable artifacts can be a skill's SKILL.md plus scripts, a pipeline's pipeline.json plus node code, or a single-file algorithm plus its description. The system being optimised need not contain an LLM; the Proposer must be able to write code.

What stands out:

  • Optimisation becomes file editing. Prompts, skills, DAG topology and node implementations all go through one mechanism because they share one property: they are files.
  • The scoring rule is the objective. The evaluator returns 0 to 1, train and validation are split, and the README insists on a held-out set rather than gains on the training split.
  • The design records edits alongside failure evidence. The deliverable includes lineage linking changes to the failure material used by the proposer. This records a rationale, not proof that the edit caused an improvement.
  • Candidate state is persisted for interruption and resumption. Candidates, runs, analyses and changelogs land in a CandidateStore. I have not tested crash recovery, partial external effects or exact replay behaviour.

Compared with: OpenEvolve is another evolutionary-code-optimisation project; its reported gains are tied to its own tasks and evaluation conditions, which I did not reproduce. This project widens the object to skills, prompts, pipeline configs and node code inside a directory, restricts the editor to a coding agent reading failure trajectories, and treats the change-to-failure mapping as part of the deliverable. These descriptions do not establish that the projects have mutually exclusive optimisation targets or that either is more effective. I only read both READMEs and ran neither.

Recent updates: No releases. On 29 October the visualiser gained an English/Chinese switch; on 28 October a trajectory-model document landed along with a note that the paper's experiment scripts and datasets will be open-sourced separately. The paper is Mara Chain (arXiv 2609.35855).

Who it's for: Teams with a repeatable, reasonably cheap evaluation whose optimisation target can be expressed as a directory of files. The docs are explicit about the mismatch cases: a handful of scalar parameters, an evaluation that is not repeatable or is very expensive, or output with strict compliance requirements (it edits files in a sandbox, so audit the permissions yourself).

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Treating auditability as a hard requirement is worth more than the evolutionary machinery itself.

Checked: README, docs/when-to-use.md, recent commits and the paper entry; not installed.

4. wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese ⭐ 407 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese

In one line: A Chinese-language course on engineering AI agents, built around Stanford CS329Z's public materials: 19 lessons, four exercises, readable offline.

What it is: 19 lessons, four hands-on exercises, Markdown sources, a single-file offline HTML reader, and scripts to build and verify publication. The order follows the engineering chain: agent landscape, LLMs for builders, RAG, tool use and function calling, orchestration, context management, memory architecture, multi-agent systems, system optimisation, evaluation engineering, data selection and quality, LLM judges, safety, coding agents, proactive agents, open problems. The README states plainly that this is an independent Chinese study guide, not an official Stanford translation, and that rights to the original course and code stay with their authors; open revisions live in a separate editorial-notes file. There is no license file at the repository root.

What stands out:

  • Evaluation is written as a specification. Lesson 13 formalises agent evaluation as a four-tuple; request, environment, stopping criteria, scorer; and lists four difficulties: non-unique solution paths, stateful environments with side effects, compounded non-determinism, and cost plus safety constraints.
  • Scaffolding is called out. The same model with a different token budget or tool set cannot be compared directly; realistic scaffolding needs controlled variables. That one line is useful when reading anyone else's leaderboard.
  • Dense per lesson. A lesson runs several thousand characters with stated learning goals, not a bullet outline.
  • Offline. The single-file HTML does not depend on the site.

Compared with: Among Chinese agent courses it chose to reproduce one course lesson by lesson rather than spread a roadmap wide; the cost is narrow coverage. Against the original English course the increment is Chinese phrasing and engineering organisation, and I did not compare coverage lesson by lesson. There is a practical constraint: the text is organised from public course materials, the repository carries no license, and rights stay with the original authors; public availability does not establish permission to redistribute or use the material commercially; check the applicable rights.

Recent updates: First release on 28 October, then per-lesson descriptions and Chinese search improvements on 31 October. Five days in: 407 stars, 45 forks.

Who it's for: Python developers who want to fill in agent engineering concepts systematically, especially evaluation and safety. If you want a runnable codebase, that is not the shape here; there are exercises, but the body is lecture material.

My take: ⭐⭐. Solid as a Chinese-language evaluation text; as an engineering reference it needs code alongside.

Checked: README, lesson 13, and the repository file list; did not run the build scripts.

5. heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills ⭐ 6,332 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills

In one line: A cross-vendor directory of agent skills; 388 entries; with six quality criteria attached.

What it is: An 82 KB README with 388 links in six languages, plus a companion site. Two halves: official and vendor directories (AI platforms and models, cloud and infrastructure, developer tools and frameworks, the Google ecosystem, business and marketing, security and web intelligence; six sections with 47 vendor groups), and community skills (16 groups covering vector databases, data and analytics, cloud storage, marketing and more). Its claim is to list skills real teams use rather than bulk-generated ones; the compatibility list names Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Windsurf.

What stands out:

  • Organised by who published it. Vendor-maintained skills come first, then third-party ones; a useful provenance distinction, not a substitute for inspecting the contents.
  • Six quality criteria. Unambiguous instructions, one focused task, a working example, documented trade-offs, SKILL.md under 500 lines, verified on the target agent. Usable directly as acceptance checks.
  • Translations are a pipeline. Commits show translated READMEs and site data synced from the main README rather than six hand-maintained copies.
  • Submissions pass an automated gate. Every pull request triggers a checker script: only README.md may change, changes must be additive, at most five lines per PR, a fixed line format, duplicate detection, the repository must exist and not be archived, it must contain a SKILL.md, have at least 20 stars and be at least 14 days old; failures get a needs-fixes label. Entries come from outside contributors, but code enforces the floor.

Compared with: Against a plain link list it adds two concrete things; six stated quality criteria and an automated gate that actually rejects submissions (the rules above are the script's rules); against each vendor's own marketplace it is a horizontal index, and its compatibility list names intended hosts. It does not establish that each listed skill was tested on every host or version. What the gate verifies is entry compliance and repository availability; it cannot verify a claim like "verified on the target agent", which still depends on the author or your own test.

Recent updates: On 2 November it synced multilingual READMEs and site data, tidied a triage batch, and added claude-code-skills-zh, motionboard, mobbin/skills and others (#641 to #647). Created on 29 December 2025; 6,332 stars since.

Who it's for: People looking for existing skills, or wanting acceptance criteria for their own. Start with the vendor sections; check third-party entries' maintenance yourself.

My take: ⭐⭐. Fine as an index, not as a quality endorsement.

Checked: README structure, the quality-standards section, the pull-request checker script and recent commits; installed no skills.

At a glance

Project What it is Most distinctive Who it's for Worth digging
RustXNG Self-hosted retrieval layer Results and page text in one request, SSRF-guarded Anyone wiring search for a local agent ⭐⭐⭐
second-brain-os Self-maintaining knowledge base Maintenance as 72 commands; a documented ingest/lint/query workflow People on file-based notes ⭐⭐⭐
AntOmniEvo Auto-evolution framework Every edit carries a failure trail, diffable and revertible Teams with a stable evaluation ⭐⭐⭐
cs329z-chinese Chinese agent course Evaluation taught as a four-tuple specification Anyone filling gaps in evaluation and safety ⭐⭐
awesome-agent-skills Skills directory A cross-vendor index with six stated acceptance criteria Finding skills, setting standards ⭐⭐

Notes from this issue

  • Agent infrastructure is being split into replaceable parts. Retrieval, knowledge bases, skill directories and evolution loops each have their own projects, and the interfaces look more like services an agent calls than interfaces a person uses. When choosing, ask about the interface shape before the feature list.
  • The projects make auditability part of their design. An evolution framework requires every edit to carry a failure trail; a knowledge base makes lint a mandatory operation. Those choices make changes easier to inspect; I have no evidence here about the authors' prior losses or the effectiveness of the checks.
  • Stating limits has become part of the documentation. One says outright that Google is unavailable in this build; another says the framework does not fit systems with only a few scalar parameters. Sentences like these help more than a performance table.

For this issue I picked five projects from GitHub Trending and topic-search candidates, mostly AI agents and developer tools. I read each project's README, release notes and recent commits; I did not install them unless an entry says so. Stars and other numbers are from GitHub as of 2026-11-02.

All five point at the same thing: infrastructure for agents; retrieval, a knowledge base, a skills directory, an evolution loop, and one course that turns evaluation into a specification.

1. sahenjp/RustXNG ⭐ 471 · Rust

GitHub: https://github.com/sahenjp/RustXNG

In one line: A self-hosted search service that returns ranked results and page text in a single request, built to be an agent's retrieval layer.

What it is: Written in Rust, AGPL-3.0-or-later, a port of SearXNG with a SearXNG-compatible response shape and a browser UI on port 8888. The repository was created on 18 October 2026 and reached v0.26.0 in two weeks, with two releases on 1 November.

What stands out:

  • Text comes back with the results. With include_raw_content=1 it returns about 32,000 characters from the top five pages, so an agent can inspect extracted text without fetching every page separately. Extraction does not establish source accuracy, completeness or permission to republish it.
  • Several upstream engines with per-engine failure handling. 226 engine types, 352 settings entries, 180 enabled by default; each engine has its own timeout, failed engines are suspended with backoff, and engines that keep returning nothing are rested.
  • The project documents default SSRF checks. The documented policy restricts fetching to public addresses. I have not tested redirects, DNS changes or the full network boundary; it is not an independent security guarantee.
  • Ops surface included. /healthz, OpenMetrics /metrics, response cache, image proxy, bot rate limiting, and idle timeout for sidecars.

Compared with: The relationship to SearXNG is a port, not a fork in spirit; compatible interface, engines carried over, plus page-text fetching, SSRF protection and a ranking pass (term coverage, site authority, identifier match). Those additions are documented by the project; I did not re-check them against SearXNG item by item. Against hosted search APIs the difference is self-hosting and text volume: the README reports a 100-question comparison on one machine, hit@1 of 79–83 versus Exa 77 and Tavily 34; about 32,000 characters per request versus about 9,000 and about 1,200; 0.01 s for a repeated query versus 0.6 s and about 1 s. Those are the project's own numbers, not my tests, and it notes they move a few points between runs.

Recent updates: v0.26.0 (1 November) published a ghcr.io image and made the English README primary; v0.25.0 the same day repositioned the project as an agent retrieval layer. All three release notes are one line about checksums, so the substance is in the commit messages.

Who it's for: Anyone who wants to host an agent-search endpoint. The metasearch service still sends queries to enabled upstream engines and fetches third-party pages; self-hosting does not make retrieval offline or eliminate third-party data exposure. Two conditions apply: Google is unavailable in this build (the WML endpoint returns 403, the HTML endpoint needs JavaScript, headless browsers get detected), so replacement engines need testing; and the license is AGPL-3.0-or-later, whose exact terms should be checked for the intended deployment. The README specifically discusses source obligations for a modified network-service version; network access alone is not a complete licence analysis.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Collapsing "found it" and "got citable text" into one request is the right subtraction; whether it replaces an existing setup depends on results without Google.

Checked: README, three release notes, recent commits and docs/COMPARISON-EXA.md; not installed.

2. undefined-ui/second-brain-os ⭐ 1,170 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/undefined-ui/second-brain-os

In one line: A plain-Markdown knowledge base an agent maintains for you, plus a course and toolkit for building that agent.

What it is: 130 pages; a guide, a seven-module agents course and five handbooks; with a toolkit of 18 skills, 72 slash commands, 6 subagents, 4 scripts, a plugin and a starter vault. MIT. Obsidian is a viewer, not a dependency. It implements the llm-wiki pattern Karpathy published as a gist on 4 April 2026: the wiki is primary and raw sources are an archive; new sources get compiled into existing pages; three operations; ingest, lint, query.

What stands out:

  • Compilation, not side-by-side summaries. A concept page is rewritten and thickened by new sources instead of becoming a list of excerpts. That is a maintenance choice; I have not measured long-term accuracy or upkeep.
  • Maintenance is a command, not a reminder. 72 slash commands cover creating pages, merging, health checks and graph export; /metrics, /health and /graph-export run from scripts inside the vault.
  • Health has script-generated indicators. The health and graph-export entry points provide observable indicators. A health score or graph export does not by itself detect every contradiction or establish that stored claims are true.
  • The resource list is dated. Every entry in resources/ carries one line on why it belongs, and the README states it was checked on 1 November 2026 with stars from that day's API.

Compared with: The README compares this file-maintenance approach with memory servers and retrieval-based context assembly. This one is a methodology document plus a copyable vault plus a command set, and its bet is that an agent maintains files through fixed operations. It names Basic Memory 1.0, ai-memory 3.0 and Hindsight 1.0 and explains how it differs; that is its own account, and I did not read those repositories. The checkable dimensions are three: whether writes leave evidence, whether pages are compiled, and whether lint actually runs.

Recent updates: No releases; main-branch iteration. On 2 November the graph recommendation moved from Kuzu to Ladybug (Kuzu was archived in October 2025; the project describes Ladybug as a continuation with embedded CSV support; I have not independently verified migration compatibility), and the README was reorganised by level with a "new this month" section. A companion site went up on 14 October.

Who it's for: People already keeping file-based notes who want an agent to take over filing and linking. It assumes Claude Code's directory conventions (.claude/skills, commands, agents); another agent means changing how they load. If you want "install it and it organises itself", this is not that; it gives process and scripts, and you still feed it the first ten sources.

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. The method matters more than the tooling, and here the method is written as executable commands.

Checked: README, the llm-wiki pattern document and recent commits; not installed.

3. ant-research/AntOmniEvo ⭐ 1,221 · Python

GitHub: https://github.com/ant-research/AntOmniEvo

In one line: A framework that treats a system's tunable parts as a directory of files, has a coding agent rewrite them from failure trajectories, and keeps the loop and the audit trail.

What it is: Python, Apache-2.0. The division of labour is "you define, the framework controls, AI does the work": you supply how to run the system, an evaluator, train/val data, a directory mapping for the tunable artifacts, and a starting point; the framework handles scheduling, budgets, selection and persistence; a coding agent acts as the Proposer. Tunable artifacts can be a skill's SKILL.md plus scripts, a pipeline's pipeline.json plus node code, or a single-file algorithm plus its description. The system being optimised need not contain an LLM; the Proposer must be able to write code.

What stands out:

  • Optimisation becomes file editing. Prompts, skills, DAG topology and node implementations all go through one mechanism because they share one property: they are files.
  • The scoring rule is the objective. The evaluator returns 0 to 1, train and validation are split, and the README insists on a held-out set rather than gains on the training split.
  • The design records edits alongside failure evidence. The deliverable includes lineage linking changes to the failure material used by the proposer. This records a rationale, not proof that the edit caused an improvement.
  • Candidate state is persisted for interruption and resumption. Candidates, runs, analyses and changelogs land in a CandidateStore. I have not tested crash recovery, partial external effects or exact replay behaviour.

Compared with: OpenEvolve is another evolutionary-code-optimisation project; its reported gains are tied to its own tasks and evaluation conditions, which I did not reproduce. This project widens the object to skills, prompts, pipeline configs and node code inside a directory, restricts the editor to a coding agent reading failure trajectories, and treats the change-to-failure mapping as part of the deliverable. These descriptions do not establish that the projects have mutually exclusive optimisation targets or that either is more effective. I only read both READMEs and ran neither.

Recent updates: No releases. On 29 October the visualiser gained an English/Chinese switch; on 28 October a trajectory-model document landed along with a note that the paper's experiment scripts and datasets will be open-sourced separately. The paper is Mara Chain (arXiv 2609.35855).

Who it's for: Teams with a repeatable, reasonably cheap evaluation whose optimisation target can be expressed as a directory of files. The docs are explicit about the mismatch cases: a handful of scalar parameters, an evaluation that is not repeatable or is very expensive, or output with strict compliance requirements (it edits files in a sandbox, so audit the permissions yourself).

My take: ⭐⭐⭐. Treating auditability as a hard requirement is worth more than the evolutionary machinery itself.

Checked: README, docs/when-to-use.md, recent commits and the paper entry; not installed.

4. wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese ⭐ 407 · HTML

GitHub: https://github.com/wanghao-SunSky/cs329z-chinese

In one line: A Chinese-language course on engineering AI agents, built around Stanford CS329Z's public materials: 19 lessons, four exercises, readable offline.

What it is: 19 lessons, four hands-on exercises, Markdown sources, a single-file offline HTML reader, and scripts to build and verify publication. The order follows the engineering chain: agent landscape, LLMs for builders, RAG, tool use and function calling, orchestration, context management, memory architecture, multi-agent systems, system optimisation, evaluation engineering, data selection and quality, LLM judges, safety, coding agents, proactive agents, open problems. The README states plainly that this is an independent Chinese study guide, not an official Stanford translation, and that rights to the original course and code stay with their authors; open revisions live in a separate editorial-notes file. There is no license file at the repository root.

What stands out:

  • Evaluation is written as a specification. Lesson 13 formalises agent evaluation as a four-tuple; request, environment, stopping criteria, scorer; and lists four difficulties: non-unique solution paths, stateful environments with side effects, compounded non-determinism, and cost plus safety constraints.
  • Scaffolding is called out. The same model with a different token budget or tool set cannot be compared directly; realistic scaffolding needs controlled variables. That one line is useful when reading anyone else's leaderboard.
  • Dense per lesson. A lesson runs several thousand characters with stated learning goals, not a bullet outline.
  • Offline. The single-file HTML does not depend on the site.

Compared with: Among Chinese agent courses it chose to reproduce one course lesson by lesson rather than spread a roadmap wide; the cost is narrow coverage. Against the original English course the increment is Chinese phrasing and engineering organisation, and I did not compare coverage lesson by lesson. There is a practical constraint: the text is organised from public course materials, the repository carries no license, and rights stay with the original authors; public availability does not establish permission to redistribute or use the material commercially; check the applicable rights.

Recent updates: First release on 28 October, then per-lesson descriptions and Chinese search improvements on 31 October. Five days in: 407 stars, 45 forks.

Who it's for: Python developers who want to fill in agent engineering concepts systematically, especially evaluation and safety. If you want a runnable codebase, that is not the shape here; there are exercises, but the body is lecture material.

My take: ⭐⭐. Solid as a Chinese-language evaluation text; as an engineering reference it needs code alongside.

Checked: README, lesson 13, and the repository file list; did not run the build scripts.

5. heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills ⭐ 6,332 · TypeScript

GitHub: https://github.com/heilcheng/awesome-agent-skills

In one line: A cross-vendor directory of agent skills; 388 entries; with six quality criteria attached.

What it is: An 82 KB README with 388 links in six languages, plus a companion site. Two halves: official and vendor directories (AI platforms and models, cloud and infrastructure, developer tools and frameworks, the Google ecosystem, business and marketing, security and web intelligence; six sections with 47 vendor groups), and community skills (16 groups covering vector databases, data and analytics, cloud storage, marketing and more). Its claim is to list skills real teams use rather than bulk-generated ones; the compatibility list names Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Windsurf.

What stands out:

  • Organised by who published it. Vendor-maintained skills come first, then third-party ones; a useful provenance distinction, not a substitute for inspecting the contents.
  • Six quality criteria. Unambiguous instructions, one focused task, a working example, documented trade-offs, SKILL.md under 500 lines, verified on the target agent. Usable directly as acceptance checks.
  • Translations are a pipeline. Commits show translated READMEs and site data synced from the main README rather than six hand-maintained copies.
  • Submissions pass an automated gate. Every pull request triggers a checker script: only README.md may change, changes must be additive, at most five lines per PR, a fixed line format, duplicate detection, the repository must exist and not be archived, it must contain a SKILL.md, have at least 20 stars and be at least 14 days old; failures get a needs-fixes label. Entries come from outside contributors, but code enforces the floor.

Compared with: Against a plain link list it adds two concrete things; six stated quality criteria and an automated gate that actually rejects submissions (the rules above are the script's rules); against each vendor's own marketplace it is a horizontal index, and its compatibility list names intended hosts. It does not establish that each listed skill was tested on every host or version. What the gate verifies is entry compliance and repository availability; it cannot verify a claim like "verified on the target agent", which still depends on the author or your own test.

Recent updates: On 2 November it synced multilingual READMEs and site data, tidied a triage batch, and added claude-code-skills-zh, motionboard, mobbin/skills and others (#641 to #647). Created on 29 December 2025; 6,332 stars since.

Who it's for: People looking for existing skills, or wanting acceptance criteria for their own. Start with the vendor sections; check third-party entries' maintenance yourself.

My take: ⭐⭐. Fine as an index, not as a quality endorsement.

Checked: README structure, the quality-standards section, the pull-request checker script and recent commits; installed no skills.

At a glance

Project What it is Most distinctive Who it's for Worth digging
RustXNG Self-hosted retrieval layer Results and page text in one request, SSRF-guarded Anyone wiring search for a local agent ⭐⭐⭐
second-brain-os Self-maintaining knowledge base Maintenance as 72 commands; a documented ingest/lint/query workflow People on file-based notes ⭐⭐⭐
AntOmniEvo Auto-evolution framework Every edit carries a failure trail, diffable and revertible Teams with a stable evaluation ⭐⭐⭐
cs329z-chinese Chinese agent course Evaluation taught as a four-tuple specification Anyone filling gaps in evaluation and safety ⭐⭐
awesome-agent-skills Skills directory A cross-vendor index with six stated acceptance criteria Finding skills, setting standards ⭐⭐

Notes from this issue

  • Agent infrastructure is being split into replaceable parts. Retrieval, knowledge bases, skill directories and evolution loops each have their own projects, and the interfaces look more like services an agent calls than interfaces a person uses. When choosing, ask about the interface shape before the feature list.
  • The projects make auditability part of their design. An evolution framework requires every edit to carry a failure trail; a knowledge base makes lint a mandatory operation. Those choices make changes easier to inspect; I have no evidence here about the authors' prior losses or the effectiveness of the checks.
  • Stating limits has become part of the documentation. One says outright that Google is unavailable in this build; another says the framework does not fit systems with only a few scalar parameters. Sentences like these help more than a performance table.

title: I built a terminal multiplexer for coding agents that works on my phone
summary:
Disclosure: drafted with AI help from my own notes and posts, and checked against the repo.

I run a lot of coding agents at once, mostly Claude Code and Codex, across several projects. Running them was never the problem. The problems were everything around them: too many windows, agents leaving hung processes behind, no way to tell which one was waiting on me, and having to remote into my desktop or SSH into a single shell to deal with any of it from my phone. Even then, a terminal on a phone couldn't show me the frontend I needed to check.

I tried Orca and herdr. Both were better than what I had. Neither had a real markdown notes editor, and neither had a phone interface I could actually work in. So I built swe-mux.

What it is

A terminal multiplexer. It runs any shell or CLI in real terminals on your own machine and serves the same live sessions to your desktop and your phone. Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and oh-my-pi get a live status (working, done, or waiting on you), searchable history and resume. Anything else runs as an ordinary terminal with everything except the status.

It's the actual terminal, not a UI wrapped around the agent. You can use it as a plain terminal, or start claude in a shell and that pane becomes an agent session.

On the desktop it's tabs and panes of sessions, notes, files and dev-server previews. Shift+Enter, Ctrl+Backspace, paste and click-to-position behave the same in every agent, shortcuts come from tmux, VS Code, Vim or Emacs presets, and images paste straight from the clipboard.

Status

Status comes from three places: the CLI's hooks, its transcript, and the terminal itself. No single one of them reliably tells "waiting on you" apart from "busy in the background", so it uses all three. You pick which events alert you and how, a sound on the desktop and a push notification on the phone, with quiet hours and separate desktop and mobile settings.

The phone

The same sessions, over your own Tailscale network, installed as a PWA. The terminal with a usable keyboard and a key rail for the keys a phone keyboard doesn't have, git diff review, files, notes, and a push notification when an agent needs a decision.

A dev server bound to 127.0.0.1 on the host is proxied through swe-mux, so the phone opens it without another port being exposed. Being able to play-test and check a frontend on the phone is what closed the development loop there for a lot of my projects. I can work from anywhere now, and I do.

Your tailnet policy is the access control. There's no separate swe-mux login, so any device your tailnet admits gets a terminal on your machine. Treat it like SSH.

Two things I use constantly

A prompt queue, so the thing I think of mid-turn waits until the agent is actually done instead of interrupting it.

Messages between sessions, so a Codex session can ask a Claude session something. I don't want my workflow tied to one provider.

Notes

Notes, and any markdown file in a project, open in the same WYSIWYG editor on desktop and phone, and they autosave. No more notes scattered across different places.

Sessions survive updates

A separate supervisor process owns the terminals, so the daemon can restart and the app can update underneath them without killing anything. I update it several times a day. My own daemon started 615 times across the 98 days its log covers, so this was never optional.

It has limits. A reboot, a power loss or the supervisor itself crashing still ends the live processes. What survives those is the transcript and enough state to resume each agent.

Limits

It was built on Windows, which is where I use it every day and the only platform with a packaged desktop app. The installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen warns on first run; the PyPI install avoids that. macOS and Linux run the daemon and use a browser. CI runs all three, and I've tested Linux myself, but I haven't lived on macOS.

There's no swe-mux account, no server of mine in the path, and no telemetry. The agents still talk to their own providers, and there's a once-a-day update check you can turn off in Settings.

Try it

The demo is the real interface with simulated agents, nothing to install.

Install with uv tool install swe-mux (or pipx install swe-mux), then run swe-mux on Windows or swemux start elsewhere. It's Apache-2.0: github.com/jatoran/swe-mux.

I've put a lot of work into the first run. Where the install or the first hour goes wrong is the feedback I want most.

title: I built QuickTube, an open-source Android video & music downloader in Jetpack Compose
summary:
I wanted one Android app that could search, watch and save videos and music without ads or accounts. Nothing I tried did all of that, so I built QuickTube, and it's free and open source (GPL-3.0).

Download: https://github.com/devgalib/QuickTube/releases/latest
Source: https://github.com/devgalib/QuickTube

What it does

  • Search and watch YouTube with live suggestions, a trending feed, a music feed, comments and an inline player.
  • Download from YouTube and 1,800+ other sites, from 144p up to 4K, or audio only as M4A / Opus.
  • Share to download: "Download with QuickTube" shows up in every app's share sheet, and the format picker pops up right over YouTube, TikTok, Facebook and other apps.
  • Built-in browser that spots the video on any page and shows a Download bar, even before you press play.
  • Playlists and channels: download all of them, or pick the videos you want, in one batch.
  • Background playback, a gallery for your downloads, and themes with accent colours.



The interesting technical bits

Merging on the phone without re-encoding. YouTube serves high-quality video and audio as separate streams. QuickTube downloads both and remuxes them into one MP4 on the device, so a 1080p download doesn't burn the battery transcoding.

HLS to MP4. Many sites play video through blob: players fed by .m3u8 playlists, sometimes AES-128 encrypted. The app fetches the segments, decrypts them where the page provides the key, and stitches them into a normal MP4.

Finding the video in a WebView. The browser reads the page's own player data, including iframe-embedded and shadow-DOM players, so the Download bar can offer every quality the page has.

The stack: Kotlin, Jetpack Compose with Material 3, a multi-module Gradle build, NewPipe Extractor for YouTube and yt-dlp for other sites.

Try it

Grab the APK from the latest release (Android 7.0+). It updates itself after the first install. Bug reports, ideas and pull requests are welcome on GitHub.

Only download content you own or have permission to save, and respect each site's terms of service. QuickTube doesn't bypass DRM and isn't affiliated with YouTube or Google.

title: We Open-Sourced Our AI Subtitle Translation Engine: Every SRT Cue In, Every Cue Out
summary:
If you've ever pasted an SRT file into an LLM and asked for a translation, you've probably seen this: you send 400 subtitle cues and get back 397. Two short lines got merged into one sentence, one line disappeared, and from that point on every translation sits on the wrong timestamp. The output looks fine at a glance, and you only notice when the dialogue on screen no longer matches what people are saying.

We hit this problem constantly while building GeekLink's subtitle translator, so we pulled the core engine out and open-sourced it under GPL-3.0: jev-subtitle-translator.

Why LLMs mangle subtitles

LLMs are trained to write fluent text, and subtitles aren't fluent text. A single sentence often spans three cues, a cue can be just "Yeah." or "—no!", and a model that's trying to be helpful will happily join fragments into natural sentences. Ask it to "keep the format" and it mostly will, until a batch of 40 cues comes back with 38 items and nothing tells you which two are gone.

Prompt engineering alone doesn't fix this. You need structure the model can't drift away from, plus validation that doesn't trust the model's output.

How the engine handles it

The pipeline looks like this:

Parse SRT and preserve every cue
        ↓
Translate ID-tagged batches
        ↓
Validate returned IDs and non-empty translations
        ↓
Retry only missing or empty IDs
        ↓
Run deterministic checks and Jev review
        ↓
Rebuild the SRT from the original cue list

A few design decisions do most of the work:

Timestamps never reach the model. The SRT is parsed locally. Subtitle numbers, order, and timestamps stay on your machine. Only the dialogue text and a stable ID per cue are sent to the model.

Structured output, not prose. Each batch is translated with JSON Schema structured output through OpenRouter, so you can use GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Grok, or any other model that supports strict schemas. Local OpenAI-compatible servers (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, llama.cpp) work too.

Retry by ID, not by batch. After every response, the engine accepts only expected IDs with unique, non-empty translations. Checked 2026-11-02

Point RisuAI's Custom API at RelaySwitch: four fields, the model id to type, and what each message costs.

The RisuAI API settings for a hosted model live in one panel: pick Custom API as the model, paste https://api.relayswitch.io/v1 in URL, your key in Key/Password, and a model id in Request Model. RisuAI calls it a custom API; older builds and most forum posts call the same thing a reverse proxy. One key reaches every model in the catalog, from the uncensored roleplay builds to Claude, billed per token from a prepaid balance.

What you need

  • RisuAI in the browser, on desktop, or the Android or iOS app.
  • A RelaySwitch key from the console (email code sign-in). Keys start with sk-relay-.
  • A balance. Top-ups start at $10, by card or crypto, with no subscription. Before the first top-up the console chat runs 12 free turns a day, so you can try a model there before you connect it.

Where the RisuAI API settings are

  1. Open the menu (the hamburger icon, top left) and choose Settings.
  2. Open Chat Bot.
  3. Click Model to open the model picker.
  4. Choose Custom API. Older releases list it as Reverse Proxy or OpenAI Reverse proxy.

The fields

The Custom API block shows these fields, in this order.

1URL: https://api.relayswitch.io/v1

2Key/Password: sk-relay-...

3Request Model: glm-5.3-uncensored

4Format: OpenAI Compatible

5Response Streaming: on

  • URL: https://api.relayswitch.io/v1, with the /v1.
  • Key/Password: your sk-relay- key. The placeholder reads "leave it blank if it hasn't password"; ours always needs the key.
  • Request Model: the exact id from the Models page, not the display name. RisuAI does not fetch a model list, so type it.
  • Format: OpenAI Compatible (the default) for every model. The other options are OpenAI Response API, Anthropic Claude, Mistral, Google Cloud and Cohere.
  • Response Streaming: on, so the reply types out as it arrives. Every model streams.

The short URL works because Autofill Request URL (Settings > Advanced Settings) is on by default: RisuAI adds /chat/completions to a URL that ends in v1. If you turned it off, paste the full endpoint, https://api.relayswitch.io/v1/chat/completions.

RisuAI has no Connect or Test button, so the first message is the test. An error shows in the chat in place of the reply.

  • 401: the key is wrong or revoked. Paste it again in Key/Password.
  • 402: the balance is empty, or the key reached its own budget. Top up or raise the budget in the console.
  • 403 scope_denied: the key is limited to a list of models and this id is not on it. Add it to the key or use another key.
  • 404 model_not_found: Request Model is not an id the catalog lists. Copy it from the Models page. route_not_found: the URL is wrong; with Autofill Request URL off, it must end in /chat/completions (or /messages on the Anthropic format).
  • 429: the key hit its requests or tokens per minute limit. Wait a few seconds and resend.
  • 503: no host could serve that model right now. Resend, or pick another model.

The API docs list every error code.

Sources

Field names, the Format options, the model picker path and the Autofill Request URL behavior are from RisuAI's repository on the main branch, read 2026-11-02: src/lang/en.ts, BotSettings.svelte, openAI/requests.ts, anthropic.ts and database.svelte.ts (Autofill Request URL defaults to on). The documentation site, docs.risuai.net, was unreachable on 2026-11-02, and the GitHub wiki is marked outdated by its maintainers.

Questions

What are the best RisuAI API settings?

Custom API as the model, URL https://api.relayswitch.io/v1, your key in Key/Password, Format OpenAI Compatible, Response Streaming on, and an id from the Models page in Request Model. Then set Max Context Size at or under that model's window; it decides most of what a message costs.

Where are the RisuAI API settings on Android?

In the same place as on the web: menu > Settings > Chat Bot > Model > Custom API. The Android and iOS app share the settings panel with the browser build, so the URL, Key/Password, Request Model and Format fields are identical.

Are the RisuAI API settings in Reddit posts still right?

The fields are, the names are not. Older posts call the option Reverse Proxy or OpenAI Reverse proxy; current builds call it Custom API in the model picker. URL, Key/Password and Request Model work the same way.

Is the RisuAI wiki on GitHub up to date?

No. The GitHub wiki is marked outdated, and docs.risuai.net was unreachable on 2026-11-02. The field names on this page come from the app source on the main branch, read the same day.

What URL goes in RisuAI custom API?

https://api.relayswitch.io/v1. With Autofill Request URL on (the default), RisuAI adds /chat/completions itself, or /messages on the Anthropic Claude format. With it off, paste https://api.relayswitch.io/v1/chat/completions.

Does RisuAI work with an OpenAI-compatible proxy?

Yes. Custom API on the OpenAI Compatible format is RisuAI's proxy setting. Any endpoint that speaks the Chat Completions format works there, including RelaySwitch.

How do I test the connection in RisuAI?

Send a message. RisuAI has no Test button and does not fetch a model list, so the first reply is the test. An error code in the chat tells you which field to fix: 401 the key, 404 the model id or the URL.

Can I use Claude in RisuAI with a custom API?

Yes. Type a Claude id in Request Model and leave Format on OpenAI Compatible, or switch Format to Anthropic Claude with the same URL and key. RelaySwitch accepts the x-api-key header RisuAI sends on that format.

How much does a RisuAI message cost?

It depends on the model and how much history goes with the message. One 2K-in / 300-out turn on GLM-5.3 Flash Uncensored costs $0.00033 today, or $0.0331 for 100. A larger Max Context Size raises the input side once the chat fills it.

Custom API as the model, URL https://api.relayswitch.io/v1, your key in Key/Password, Format OpenAI Compatible, Response Streaming on, and an id from the Models page in Request Model. Then set Max Context Size at or under that model's window; it decides most of what a message costs.

In the same place as on the web: menu > Settings > Chat Bot > Model > Custom API. The Android and iOS app share the settings panel with the browser build, so the URL, Key/Password, Request Model and Format fields are identical.

The fields are, the names are not. Older posts call the option Reverse Proxy or OpenAI Reverse proxy; current builds call it Custom API in the model picker. URL, Key/Password and Request Model work the same way.

Send a message. RisuAI has no Test button and does not fetch a model list, so the first reply is the test. An error code in the chat tells you which field to fix: 401 the key, 404 the model id or the URL.

title: I built a CLI package manager for macOS because brew list hid 145 dependencies
summary:
I ran brew list on my Mac and got 188 names.

I knew maybe 40 of them. The other 145 were libraries that arrived because
something else needed them — abseil, icu4c, isl, highway. Nothing told
me which was which, what anything did, how much space it took, or which command
would remove it safely.

That is the problem Cydia and Sileo solved on a jailbroken iPhone: one list,
searchable, with a Remove button. macOS never got that view. So I built one.

What Dronagiri does

Dronagiri is a terminal app that reads the package databases of Homebrew, npm,
pipx, Cargo, RubyGems and go install, then puts everything in one sortable
table:

  • real on-disk size, measured with one batched du
  • install date
  • one-line description and homepage
  • last-used evidence from Spotlight and timestamped shell history
  • popularity from Homebrew's public analytics
  • dependencies in their own tab, each labelled with the packages that need it
  • broken entries: packages a manager still lists whose files are gone

The part I use most is the Mine / Dependencies split. brew list treats the
40 tools I chose and the 145 libraries they dragged in as one flat list.
Dronagiri separates them.

The hard parts

Two things were harder than the UI.

Dependencies lie. Homebrew's JSON lists declared dependencies, which is wrong
surprisingly often. Dronagiri asks brew deps for the actual runtime
linkage, then inverts the graph. That is why it can say "needed by ffmpeg, mpv"
instead of guessing.

"Last used" is mostly unknowable. APFS mounts with noatime, so access
times never change. Most shells do not timestamp their history. Dronagiri uses
Spotlight's kMDItemLastUsedDate for .app bundles and timestamped shell
history for commands. When neither exists, it says never — meaning no trace,
not proof you never ran it. The detail panel spells that out.

Safety

Deletion is deliberately inconvenient. Select rows with space, press d, and
confirm twice in bordered dialogs. The first window lists every package and the
space freed; the second is a last-chance warning. Removal is delegated to the
manager that installed the package. No --force, no --ignore-dependencies, no
private APIs.

Try it 

go install github.com/MasterShivnath007/dronagiri@latest
dronagiri

Or download a binary for Apple Silicon or Intel from the releases page. It is
MIT-licensed, macOS 13+, and there is no telemetry or account.

  • Website and install guide: https://mastershivnath007.github.io/dronagiri/
  • Source: https://github.com/MasterShivnath007/dronagiri
  • The brew list comparison: https://mastershivnath007.github.io/dronagiri/#compare

If you try it, I would like to know what your Mine/Dependencies split looks
like — and which package you were surprised to find.
