title: markgate: Mechanically Catch Coding Agent Slip-ups and Enforce Non-Command Tasks
summary:
I built an OSS tool called markgate that mechanically catches and enforces two kinds of gaps: when a Coding Agent (Claude Code, etc.) accidentally forgets to call a Skill that runs build or tests after implementation and commits anyway, and when AI tasks that can't be reduced to a command — like a /check-docs Skill — can't be enforced through hooks.

markgate

NOTE: markgate is meant to run inside a git repository.

markgate

markgate is a CLI tool that acts as an enforcement layer wedged between the Coding Agent and your hooks. By mechanically catching and enforcing the Coding Agent's mistakes and omissions, it addresses the following three failure patterns.

Pattern Failure pattern it addresses Solution
1 Catching forgotten calls and avoiding duplicate execution markgate run
2 Enforcing non-command tasks markgate set + markgate verify
3 Scoping multiple tasks + aggregate verify composes in .markgate.yml

Below, we'll walk through each pattern in turn.

Pattern 1: Catching Forgotten Calls and Avoiding Duplicate Execution (markgate run)

Suppose you have an implementation skill, and a check skill (/check) that runs after it.

/check runs verifications against the implemented code. The things you want to guarantee against your implementation will vary by project — tests, typecheck, lint, format, build, documentation consistency, coverage generation, image scans, and so on.

However, even if you tell the Coding Agent "run /check after implementing", the Coding Agent can forget and silently skip the step. When that happens, your code gets committed without the checks you wanted to run.

So, you set up a pre-commit hook to forcibly run the equivalent of /check.

But the Coding Agent doesn't always forget. In fact, forgetting is rare — usually it runs /check just fine.

That leads to "the skill already ran it → the hook runs it again", a duplicate execution.

If /check is heavy, this slows down what should be a fast Coding Agent development cycle. If it's light you might not notice, but running it frequently still wastes a non-trivial amount of time.

Furthermore, if you skip the check after the implementation skill and put all check logic only in the hook, you can't run checks when you're not yet ready to commit. Running a post-edit hook on every file change isn't a great answer either, since the checks then run on every edit and that takes time.

Solved with markgate run

markgate keeps both the /check skill and the hook in place, and makes it so that the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check.

In other words, when the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen.

Usage

The basic flow is no config file required — just call the command.

For example, suppose your /check skill and pre-commit hook from above both run pnpm build. And suppose the pre-commit hook is wired up via Claude Code's PreToolUse hook firing on git commit*.

1. /check skill

In the /check skill that runs first, wrap the pnpm build command using markgate run -- .

// ... inside the skill definition
- pnpm build
+ markgate run -- pnpm build

2. hook

In the pre-commit hook, rewrite pnpm build to markgate run -- pnpm build in the same way.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
-     "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "pnpm build" }]
+     "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "markgate run -- pnpm build" }]
    }]
  }
}

With just this, you get the behavior where the hook fires only when the Coding Agent forgets /check, running pnpm build. When the Coding Agent runs /check properly, the latter hook is skipped, so duplicate execution doesn't happen.

Pattern 2: Enforcing Non-command Tasks (set + verify)

Up to this point, markgate run has meant writing the target command (pnpm build, etc.) directly into the hook configuration.

In practice, though, there are also tasks that can't be reduced to a command. For example, "is the documentation consistent with src?", "does the PR description match the diff?", "is naming consistent with the existing code?" — these are reviews that need LLM judgment and can't be expressed as a shell command.

You want to run this kind of LLM task in the Coding Agent's own session, because you want to leverage the context the Coding Agent has built up (conversation history, open files, past decisions). Technically, you could launch a separate session from a hook via claude -p, but since the context isn't shared, it doesn't act as a continuation of the work so far. As a result, the hook alone can't tell whether the Coding Agent ran an LLM task like /check-docs, which means there's no way to enforce it.

Building a Gate with set + verify

That's where the gate pattern — combining markgate set and markgate verify — comes in. The check itself stays on the skill side; set records "the moment the check passed" as a marker, and on the hook side, verify acts as a gate that judges whether "the recorded marker matches the current marker".

  • markgate set: records the moment the check passed as a marker
  • markgate verify: exits 0 if the recorded marker matches the current marker, and exits 1 to stop things if they don't match

Since the marker records the code state at the time of set, when the code changes afterward the recorded marker and the current marker no longer match, and verify stops things (we'll cover what's inside a marker later).

Usage

At the end of where the check actually runs (a skill like /check-docs), call markgate set. On the hook side, just call markgate verify.

# At the end of the /check-docs skill definition
markgate set

// .claude/settings.json (hook side)
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "markgate verify || { echo 'run /check-docs' >&2; exit 1; }" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The whole chain of check operations stays defined on the skill side, and the hook just looks at the marker. If the marker is missing or doesn't match the code, the hook blocks with exit 1, and the Coding Agent gets both the error and a hint (run /check-docs), so when the gate blocks things, recovery can be left to the Coding Agent and it can loop again.

Catching Both "First-time Non-command Triggers" and "Slip-ups"

This gate pattern is effective in both of the following cases.

  1. First-time non-command trigger: The Coding Agent doesn't even know /check-docs exists and tries to commit. → Since there's no marker, the hook blocks, and after reading the error message (run /check-docs), the Coding Agent runs /check-docs for the first time.
  2. Slip-up: The Coding Agent runs /check-docs and the marker is set. But later, when the code is edited again and you want to re-check, the Coding Agent forgets to re-run /check-docs. → Since the marker no longer matches the code, the hook blocks and prompts the Coding Agent to re-run.

In short, markgate uniformly catches both never-run-before cases and failure to re-run after a slip-up, using the same logic: "does the marker match the current code state?".

Pattern 3: Scoping and Aggregate Verify (.markgate.yml + composes)

So far we've assumed "one skill, one hook", but in practice you often have multiple checks lined up.

For example, suppose at pre-commit you want to run light checks (check: typecheck / lint / build / unit test) plus a heavier check that uses an LLM to verify documentation consistency (docs).

The problem here is wasted runs. If you bundle them into a single gate, even on a commit that only touches tests, the LLM consistency check runs even though nothing in the documentation-related files changed. That would mean re-running the heavy LLM check every time you change any code, which isn't practical.

Giving Each Task Its Own Scope

That's where .markgate.yml comes in: give each check its "own scope" (= the set of files specified in include). Whether a re-run is needed is judged by whether the code change falls within that scope.

On top of that, using composes to create an aggregate gate that bundles multiple gates means the hook side can judge "do all the bundled gates match the current code?" with just a single line of verify.

Usage

Create a .markgate.yml (markgate init generates a template).

# .markgate.yml
gates:
  check:
    hash: files # only the files specified in include are hashed
    include:
      - "src/**"
      - "tests/**"
      - "package.json"
  docs:
    hash: files
    include:
      - "src/**" # changes in src also affect docs, so include in both
      - "docs/**"
      - "README.md"
  pre-commit:
    composes: [check, docs] # aggregate gate: AND of check and docs

From the skill side, specify the gate name as an argument and set each gate individually.

# At the end of the /check skill definition
pnpm typecheck && pnpm lint && pnpm test && markgate set check

# At the end of the /check-docs skill definition
markgate set docs

Then, in the pre-commit hook, verify the pre-commit aggregate gate in a single line. When it doesn't match, markgate status pre-commit shows "which gate doesn't match", and the Coding Agent reads that and re-loops the corresponding skill.

// .claude/settings.json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "markgate verify pre-commit || { markgate status pre-commit >&2; exit 1; }" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The key point is that only the checks needed for the edited scope get re-run. Each gate's marker only hashes the files in its own include, so on a commit that only touches one side's scope, the other gate's marker stays the same as when it was set and still matches, meaning no re-run is needed.

For example, a commit that only modifies tests re-runs only the light checks; a commit that only touches files outside any include (CI config, etc.) skips both.

Edited files check docs Checks that need to re-run
tests/** only stale fresh light checks only
docs/** / README.md only fresh stale heavy check only
src/** stale stale both
None of the above (CI config, editor config, etc.) fresh fresh none (commit passes)

Note that the pre-commit aggregate gate in this example is designed without a command of its own; it just performs the AND judgment — fresh if all bundled gates are fresh, stale if any one is stale. This shape — without its own command — can't be written with markgate run (which wraps a single command); only the gate pattern (set + verify) can express it.

Other Use Case Examples

Beyond the basic usage above, markgate has various advanced patterns.

  • Check documentation consistency before creating a PR (/check-docs → gh pr create hook)
  • Vulnerability scan before pushing an image (trivy image → docker push hook)
  • Generate a coverage report before pushing (go test -cover → git push hook)
  • Ensure E2E tests have just been re-run before merging a PR (pnpm test:e2e → gh pr merge hook)

How It Works: Managing State with Markers

Let's look at what the "marker" we've been mentioning is actually made of.

markgate works by saving the "state" at the time the target command (or task) succeeded as a marker, and on the next call of the same command (or task), if the marker matches the current state, the run is skipped; if not, it runs (markgate run) / blocks (markgate verify).

In practice, this "state" is a hash of the code content. You can choose between two hash targets: "a specific set of files" (hash: files + include) or "the repository's git status as a whole" (hash: git-tree, the default). Either way, as long as the code content hasn't changed, the command is skipped.

# First run: no marker yet, so pnpm build runs and a marker is saved on success
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.2s

# Second run: no file changes → execution is skipped
$ markgate run -- pnpm build

# After editing a file: the marker is invalidated, so the command runs again
$ echo '// fix typo' >> src/foo.ts
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.1s

By default, the marker file is stored inside .git (.git/markgate/default.json), so you don't need to create a marker file yourself, and it isn't tracked by git even without an explicit .gitignore entry. (There's also an option to explicitly change the marker file path and share markers between local and CI; see the README for that.)

Installation 

# Homebrew
brew install go-to-k/tap/markgate

# shell script
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-to-k/markgate/main/install.sh | bash

# go install
go install github.com/go-to-k/markgate/cmd/markgate@latest

# mise (ubi backend)
mise use "ubi:go-to-k/markgate@0.3.3"

Using markgate from Other Hook Managers

So far I've used the Claude Code hook as the example, but markgate is hook-manager agnostic. With husky / lefthook / the pre-commit framework, or any other hook manager, you can use it just by writing a single line of markgate run -- .

# .husky/pre-commit
markgate run -- pnpm test

# lefthook.yml
pre-commit:
  commands:
    check:
      run: markgate run -- pnpm test

# .pre-commit-config.yaml (pre-commit framework)
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: markgate-check
        name: markgate check
        entry: markgate run -- pnpm test
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false

Final Thoughts

Personally, I think this has turned into a tool I'll lean on in the AI era. In particular, the idea of "mechanically catching AI mistakes and omissions" feels like one of the important points when working with AI.

For the other features (exclude / state_dir settings in .markgate.yml, sharing markers between local and CI, strict gate dependencies via requires, etc.), see the README in the GitHub repository. If you like it, I'd be glad if you'd give the repository a ⭐.

Also, as a project that actually uses markgate in practice, there's cdkd (CDK Direct) — a from-scratch rewrite of the AWS CDK CLI that's made it blazingly fast. Nearly all of the implementation is delegated to a Coding Agent, and markgate mechanically backs that up against missed runs and non-command tasks. Take a look if you're interested.

For example, suppose at pre-commit you want to run light checks (check: typecheck / lint / build / unit test) plus a heavier check that uses an LLM to verify documentation consistency (docs).

The problem here is wasted runs. If you bundle them into a single gate, even on a commit that only touches tests, the LLM consistency check runs even though nothing in the documentation-related files changed. That would mean re-running the heavy LLM check every time you change any code, which isn't practical.

Giving Each Task Its Own Scope

That's where .markgate.yml comes in: give each check its "own scope" (= the set of files specified in include). Whether a re-run is needed is judged by whether the code change falls within that scope.

On top of that, using composes to create an aggregate gate that bundles multiple gates means the hook side can judge "do all the bundled gates match the current code?" with just a single line of verify.

Usage

Create a .markgate.yml (markgate init generates a template).

# .markgate.yml
gates:
  check:
    hash: files # only the files specified in include are hashed
    include:
      - "src/**"
      - "tests/**"
      - "package.json"
  docs:
    hash: files
    include:
      - "src/**" # changes in src also affect docs, so include in both
      - "docs/**"
      - "README.md"
  pre-commit:
    composes: [check, docs] # aggregate gate: AND of check and docs

From the skill side, specify the gate name as an argument and set each gate individually.

# At the end of the /check skill definition
pnpm typecheck && pnpm lint && pnpm test && markgate set check

# At the end of the /check-docs skill definition
markgate set docs

Then, in the pre-commit hook, verify the pre-commit aggregate gate in a single line. When it doesn't match, markgate status pre-commit shows "which gate doesn't match", and the Coding Agent reads that and re-loops the corresponding skill.

// .claude/settings.json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "if": "Bash(git commit*)",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "markgate verify pre-commit || { markgate status pre-commit >&2; exit 1; }" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The key point is that only the checks needed for the edited scope get re-run. Each gate's marker only hashes the files in its own include, so on a commit that only touches one side's scope, the other gate's marker stays the same as when it was set and still matches, meaning no re-run is needed.

For example, a commit that only modifies tests re-runs only the light checks; a commit that only touches files outside any include (CI config, etc.) skips both.

Edited files check docs Checks that need to re-run
tests/** only stale fresh light checks only
docs/** / README.md only fresh stale heavy check only
src/** stale stale both
None of the above (CI config, editor config, etc.) fresh fresh none (commit passes)

Note that the pre-commit aggregate gate in this example is designed without a command of its own; it just performs the AND judgment — fresh if all bundled gates are fresh, stale if any one is stale. This shape — without its own command — can't be written with markgate run (which wraps a single command); only the gate pattern (set + verify) can express it.

Other Use Case Examples

Beyond the basic usage above, markgate has various advanced patterns.

  • Check documentation consistency before creating a PR (/check-docs → gh pr create hook)
  • Vulnerability scan before pushing an image (trivy image → docker push hook)
  • Generate a coverage report before pushing (go test -cover → git push hook)
  • Ensure E2E tests have just been re-run before merging a PR (pnpm test:e2e → gh pr merge hook)

How It Works: Managing State with Markers

Let's look at what the "marker" we've been mentioning is actually made of.

markgate works by saving the "state" at the time the target command (or task) succeeded as a marker, and on the next call of the same command (or task), if the marker matches the current state, the run is skipped; if not, it runs (markgate run) / blocks (markgate verify).

In practice, this "state" is a hash of the code content. You can choose between two hash targets: "a specific set of files" (hash: files + include) or "the repository's git status as a whole" (hash: git-tree, the default). Either way, as long as the code content hasn't changed, the command is skipped.

# First run: no marker yet, so pnpm build runs and a marker is saved on success
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.2s

# Second run: no file changes → execution is skipped
$ markgate run -- pnpm build

# After editing a file: the marker is invalidated, so the command runs again
$ echo '// fix typo' >> src/foo.ts
$ markgate run -- pnpm build
building...
passed in 7.1s

By default, the marker file is stored inside .git (.git/markgate/default.json), so you don't need to create a marker file yourself, and it isn't tracked by git even without an explicit .gitignore entry. (There's also an option to explicitly change the marker file path and share markers between local and CI; see the README for that.)

Installation 

# Homebrew
brew install go-to-k/tap/markgate

# shell script
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/go-to-k/markgate/main/install.sh | bash

# go install
go install github.com/go-to-k/markgate/cmd/markgate@latest

# mise (ubi backend)
mise use "ubi:go-to-k/markgate@0.3.3"

Using markgate from Other Hook Managers

So far I've used the Claude Code hook as the example, but markgate is hook-manager agnostic. With husky / lefthook / the pre-commit framework, or any other hook manager, you can use it just by writing a single line of markgate run -- .

# .husky/pre-commit
markgate run -- pnpm test

# lefthook.yml
pre-commit:
  commands:
    check:
      run: markgate run -- pnpm test

# .pre-commit-config.yaml (pre-commit framework)
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: markgate-check
        name: markgate check
        entry: markgate run -- pnpm test
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false

Final Thoughts

Personally, I think this has turned into a tool I'll lean on in the AI era. In particular, the idea of "mechanically catching AI mistakes and omissions" feels like one of the important points when working with AI.

For the other features (exclude / state_dir settings in .markgate.yml, sharing markers between local and CI, strict gate dependencies via requires, etc.), see the README in the GitHub repository. If you like it, I'd be glad if you'd give the repository a ⭐.

Also, as a project that actually uses markgate in practice, there's cdkd (CDK Direct) — a from-scratch rewrite of the AWS CDK CLI that's made it blazingly fast. Nearly all of the implementation is delegated to a Coding Agent, and markgate mechanically backs that up against missed runs and non-command tasks. Take a look if you're interested.

title: SillyTavern LLM settings for an OpenAI-compatible API
summary:
Checked 2026-11-02

Connect SillyTavern to RelaySwitch as a Custom (OpenAI-compatible) Chat Completion source, then set the four samplers that reach the model, a Context Size that fits it, and reasoning.

Most SillyTavern LLM settings guides assume a local backend, where every sampler on the panel goes to the model. A hosted OpenAI-compatible API works differently. SillyTavern sends a short list of standard parameters, hides the rest, and leaves Context Size for you to set by hand.

This guide connects SillyTavern to https://api.relayswitch.io/v1, shows exactly which settings travel with each message, and sets Context Size per model from the live catalog. Every message bills per token from a prepaid balance, so the last sections price a message on each model in the table.

Looking for a SillyTavern proxy? For a model backend, that is the Custom (OpenAI-compatible) source below: a URL and a key that answer in the OpenAI format, or the Claude source's Proxy Server URL for the Anthropic format. It is not requestProxy in config.yaml, which sends SillyTavern's own outgoing traffic through a network proxy, and not the Reverse proxying page in the admin docs, which puts Traefik in front of SillyTavern for remote access.

What you need

  • SillyTavern installed and running. The steps follow the release branch.
  • A RelaySwitch key from the console (email code sign-in). Keys start with sk-relay-.
  • A balance. Top-ups start at $10, by card or crypto, with no subscription. Before the first top-up the console chat runs 12 free turns a day, so you can try a model before connecting it here.

Connect the Custom source

  1. Open API Connections (the plug icon in the top bar).
  2. Set API to Chat Completion.
  3. Set Chat Completion Source to Custom (OpenAI-compatible).
  4. Custom Endpoint (Base URL): https://api.relayswitch.io/v1. Keep the /v1. SillyTavern adds the rest; its docs put it plainly: "Do NOT add the /chat/completions suffix."
  5. Custom API Key: your key. SillyTavern hides it after you connect.
  6. Click Connect. The Available Models dropdown fills from /v1/models. Pick a model there, or type its id in Enter a Model ID.
  7. Click Test Message. It sends one short request, which bills like any other.

text

1API: Chat Completion

2Chat Completion Source: Custom (OpenAI-compatible)

3Custom Endpoint (Base URL): https://api.relayswitch.io/v1

4Custom API Key: sk-relay-...

5Enter a Model ID: claude-sonnet-5-5

Use the id the Models page prints, such as claude-sonnet-5-5, not the display name.

The Anthropic format: Claude source with a reverse proxy

SillyTavern can also send the Anthropic Messages format, through its Claude source. The reverse proxy block sits in the same connection panel; SillyTavern's docs do not cover it, so the labels here are from the UI.

  1. Set Chat Completion Source to Claude.
  2. Proxy Server URL: https://api.relayswitch.io/v1. SillyTavern adds /messages.
  3. Proxy Password: your sk-relay- key. The field's note says it is used as the password for the proxy instead of an API key, and the Claude API key field above it is ignored once a proxy is set.
  4. Pick the model in Claude Model, then click Connect.

2Chat Completion Source: Claude

3Proxy Server URL: https://api.relayswitch.io/v1

4Proxy Password: sk-relay-...

5Claude Model: claude-sonnet-4-6

Prompt Post-Processing

Prompt Post-Processing, in the connection panel under the Custom source, reshapes the message list before it leaves SillyTavern. The options, as the panel lists them:

  • None
  • Merge consecutive roles (with tools)
  • Semi-strict (alternating roles; with tools)
  • Strict (user first, alternating roles; with tools)
  • Merge consecutive roles (no tools)
  • Semi-strict (alternating roles; no tools)
  • Strict (user first, alternating roles; no tools)
  • Single user message (no tools)

Leave it on None unless a model complains. The merge options join back-to-back messages from the same role; Semi-strict also keeps user and assistant turns alternating. Pick Strict when a model answers a 400 about roles or message order: a character chat opens on the card's greeting, an assistant message, and Strict puts a user message first. The "no tools" variants drop function calling; keep a "with tools" one if you use tool calls.

SillyTavern LLM settings that reach the model

With a Custom source, the AI Response Configuration panel shows Temperature, Frequency Penalty, Presence Penalty, Top P, Seed and Max Response Length (tokens). Those are the standard Chat Completions parameters. SillyTavern's server builds this body for every message:

json

1{

2 "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5",

3 "messages": [ ... ],

4 "temperature": 1,

5 "top_p": 1,

6 "frequency_penalty": 0,

7 "presence_penalty": 0,

8 "max_tokens": 300,

9 "stream": true

10}

Custom stopping strings add a stop list, a Seed of 0 or more adds seed, and Multiple swipes per generation adds n. The API forwards all of these to the model unchanged. A model that refuses one answers with a 400 error.

Top K, Min P, Top A, Repetition Penalty, DRY, XTC, Mirostat and the other Text Completion samplers do not appear for a Custom source, and SillyTavern does not send them. Settings you made for a local backend have no effect here. To send one anyway, open Additional Parameters in the connection panel and add it under Include Body Parameters as YAML:

yaml

1min_p: 0.05

2repetition_penalty: 1.05

3reasoning_effort: high

The API passes extra fields through as well. Whether a model applies min_p or repetition_penalty depends on the model; the four standard samplers are the ones to tune first. To stop SillyTavern sending a field a model rejects, list it under Exclude Body Parameters:

yaml

1- frequency_penalty

2- presence_penalty

Starting points for long-form fiction: Temperature 0.8 to 1.0, Top P 0.95, Frequency Penalty 0.1 to 0.3 against repeated phrases, Presence Penalty 0 to 0.3 to push new topics. Change one at a time and swipe a few replies before judging.

Context Size per model

Context Size (tokens) is the most SillyTavern sends as the prompt: card, system prompt and chat history, minus the response length. A fresh install starts Chat Completion at 4,095 tokens of context and 300 response tokens. On a hosted model with a far larger window, that drops older messages long before the model needs it to.

SillyTavern does not read a context window from a Custom source. The slider goes past any model's limit, so set it from the Context column in the table below. Set it too high and a long chat fails once the prompt passes the model's window; Euryale 70B v2.3 stops at 20K tokens.

Context Size is also the cost dial. Once a chat fills it, every message sends that many input tokens, so a 32K setting costs several times more per message than a short chat on the same model. The costed example below prices both.

Reasoning

Request model reasoning in the AI Response Configuration panel shows a model's reasoning as a collapsible block above the reply when the model returns it in a separate field. For a model that writes its reasoning inline between tags, turn on Auto-Parse under Advanced Formatting > Reasoning instead.

Reasoning Effort on a Custom source is sent only for model ids SillyTavern knows from OpenAI, such as gpt-5.5. For any other model, put reasoning_effort: high (or low, medium) under Include Body Parameters. The API passes it to the model, and models with an effort setting use it.

Reasoning tokens are output tokens. They count against Max Response Length and bill at the output rate, even when the block stays collapsed. If replies come back empty or cut off, raise Max Response Length; SillyTavern's docs suggest 1024 to 4096 for reasoning models.

Which models to pick

Four general models and 2 the catalog tags for fiction and character dialogue (Gemma 4 31B Fabled, Euryale 70B v2.3). Prices are per million tokens. The message columns assume 3,000 tokens in (card plus recent history) and 300 out, the default response length.

Model Context Input Output Per message 100 messages
Claude Sonnet 5.5 1M tokens $1.20 $3.00 $0.0045 $0.45
GPT-5.5 1.1M tokens $1.80 $9.00 $0.0081 $0.81
DeepSeek V4 Pro 0423 1M tokens $0.792 $2.376 $0.0031 $0.3089
GLM 5.3 1M tokens $0.3276 $1.0296 $0.0013 $0.1292
Gemma 4 31B Fabled 262K tokens $0.35 $1.575 $0.0015 $0.1523
Euryale 70B v2.3 20K tokens $1.972 $1.972 $0.0065 $0.6508

USD, read from the RelaySwitch catalog when this page was built. Context is the developer's stated window; set Context Size at or under it.

The general models carry the largest context windows. The fiction-tuned builds are trained on stories and dialogue and have smaller windows, so check the Context column before you raise Context Size. The roleplay chat runs character cards in the browser on the same key, and the character card guide explains what each card field costs in tokens.

What a chat costs

Early in a chat on Claude Sonnet 5.5, a message sends about 3,000 tokens and gets 300 back: $0.0045 each, or $0.45 for 100 messages.

Later, with Context Size at 32K and the history filling it, each message sends 32,000 tokens: $0.0393 each, or $3.93 for 100. The same 100 full-context messages on GLM 5.3 come to $1.08.

Swipes, Continue and Test Message are requests too, each billed the same way. When the model reports cached input tokens, they bill at its cached rate, which lowers the cost of a long chat that resends the same history. The console's Usage page lists every request with its tokens and charge. The pricing page has the full billing rules.

Errors and fixes

List the models your key can call, from the machine that runs SillyTavern:

bash

1curl https://api.relayswitch.io/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-relay-..."

  • 401: the key is wrong or revoked. Paste it again in Custom API Key and click Connect.
  • 402: the balance is too low. Top up in the console; the next message goes through.
  • 404: the model id is not in the catalog. Pick it from Available Models instead of typing it.
  • 429: the key hit its rate limit. Wait a few seconds before the next swipe.
  • A 400 naming a parameter: the model refuses that field. Add it to Exclude Body Parameters, or remove it from Include Body Parameters.
  • A 400 about roles or message order: some models want alternating user and assistant turns. Set Prompt Post-Processing in the connection panel to Semi-strict, or Strict if the first message must be the user's.
  • Connection fails or the model list stays empty: the URL is missing /v1 or ends in /chat/completions. Use https://api.relayswitch.io/v1 exactly.
  • Empty or cut-off replies: a reasoning model used up Max Response Length before it wrote the reply. Raise it.
  • Old messages forgotten: Context Size is still at 4,095. Raise it toward the model's window.

The API docs list every error code.

Sources

Menu paths and field names are from SillyTavern's docs, read 2026-10-27: Chat Completions, Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Common Settings and Reasoning. The request body, the default context and response sizes, and which samplers show for a Custom source are from SillyTavern's source on the release branch, read the same day. The Claude source's reverse proxy block, its Claude Model dropdown and the Prompt Post-Processing options are from SillyTavern's UI on the release branch, read 2026-11-02. For a chat client with a model allowlist and per-user keys, see the Open WebUI guide.

Questions

What are the best SillyTavern LLM settings?

On a hosted OpenAI-compatible API, start with Temperature 0.8 to 1.0, Top P 0.95, Frequency Penalty 0.1 to 0.3 and Presence Penalty 0 to 0.3, and set Context Size to the model's window from the Models page. Those four samplers are the ones a Custom source sends; tune them before anything else.

What does presence_penalty do in SillyTavern?

presence_penalty lowers the chance of any token that already appeared in the context, once, however often it appeared. It nudges the model toward new words and topics. frequency_penalty scales with how often a token appeared, so it targets repeated phrases. Both go to the model on a Custom source; 0 turns them off.

Do DRY settings work with an OpenAI-compatible API?

Not from the panel. DRY, XTC, Min P and Top K are Text Completion samplers, and SillyTavern does not send them for a Custom Chat Completion source. You can add a field under Additional Parameters > Include Body Parameters; the API forwards it, and whether the model applies it depends on the model.

What temperature should I use for roleplay?

Between 0.7 and 1.0 for most hosted models. Lower keeps a character consistent; higher gives more varied replies and more drift. If replies start to wander off the scene, lower temperature or Top P before adding penalties.

How much does a SillyTavern message cost?

It depends on the model and on how much history goes with each message. With 3,000 tokens in and 300 out, a message on Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $0.0045 today and on GLM 5.3 $0.0013. A larger Context Size raises the input side once the chat fills it.

What is a SillyTavern proxy?

Usually a model backend: a URL and a key that answer in the OpenAI or Anthropic format. In SillyTavern that is the Custom (OpenAI-compatible) source, or the Claude source with a Proxy Server URL. The config.yaml requestProxy setting is something else, a network proxy for SillyTavern's own traffic, and so is the reverse proxy you put in front of SillyTavern for remote access.

Is there a free SillyTavern proxy?

Not here. RelaySwitch is prepaid from $10 by card or crypto, billed per token. Before the first top-up the console chat gives 12 free turns a day to try models, in the browser, not through SillyTavern.

Does SillyTavern need the /v1 at the end?

Yes. Use https://api.relayswitch.io/v1 as the Custom Endpoint (Base URL) or Proxy Server URL. SillyTavern adds /chat/completions (or /messages on the Claude source) after it, and a URL without /v1 or with the suffix already on it fails to connect.

Can I use the Claude source with a custom URL?

Yes. Set Chat Completion Source to Claude, put https://api.relayswitch.io/v1 in Proxy Server URL and your sk-relay- key in Proxy Password. The model comes from the Claude Model dropdown, which lists fixed ids; for a Claude id it does not list, use the Custom source and type the id.

With a Custom source, the AI Response Configuration panel shows Temperature, Frequency Penalty, Presence Penalty, Top P, Seed and Max Response Length (tokens). Those are the standard Chat Completions parameters. SillyTavern's server builds this body for every message:

json

1{

2 "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5",

3 "messages": [ ... ],

4 "temperature": 1,

5 "top_p": 1,

6 "frequency_penalty": 0,

7 "presence_penalty": 0,

8 "max_tokens": 300,

9 "stream": true

10}

Custom stopping strings add a stop list, a Seed of 0 or more adds seed, and Multiple swipes per generation adds n. The API forwards all of these to the model unchanged. A model that refuses one answers with a 400 error.

Top K, Min P, Top A, Repetition Penalty, DRY, XTC, Mirostat and the other Text Completion samplers do not appear for a Custom source, and SillyTavern does not send them. Settings you made for a local backend have no effect here. To send one anyway, open Additional Parameters in the connection panel and add it under Include Body Parameters as YAML:

yaml

1min_p: 0.05

2repetition_penalty: 1.05

3reasoning_effort: high

The API passes extra fields through as well. Whether a model applies min_p or repetition_penalty depends on the model; the four standard samplers are the ones to tune first. To stop SillyTavern sending a field a model rejects, list it under Exclude Body Parameters:

yaml

1- frequency_penalty

2- presence_penalty

Starting points for long-form fiction: Temperature 0.8 to 1.0, Top P 0.95, Frequency Penalty 0.1 to 0.3 against repeated phrases, Presence Penalty 0 to 0.3 to push new topics. Change one at a time and swipe a few replies before judging.

Context Size per model

Context Size (tokens) is the most SillyTavern sends as the prompt: card, system prompt and chat history, minus the response length. A fresh install starts Chat Completion at 4,095 tokens of context and 300 response tokens. On a hosted model with a far larger window, that drops older messages long before the model needs it to.

SillyTavern does not read a context window from a Custom source. The slider goes past any model's limit, so set it from the Context column in the table below. Set it too high and a long chat fails once the prompt passes the model's window; Euryale 70B v2.3 stops at 20K tokens.

Context Size is also the cost dial. Once a chat fills it, every message sends that many input tokens, so a 32K setting costs several times more per message than a short chat on the same model. The costed example below prices both.

Reasoning

Request model reasoning in the AI Response Configuration panel shows a model's reasoning as a collapsible block above the reply when the model returns it in a separate field. For a model that writes its reasoning inline between tags, turn on Auto-Parse under Advanced Formatting > Reasoning instead.

Reasoning Effort on a Custom source is sent only for model ids SillyTavern knows from OpenAI, such as gpt-5.5. For any other model, put reasoning_effort: high (or low, medium) under Include Body Parameters. The API passes it to the model, and models with an effort setting use it.

Reasoning tokens are output tokens. They count against Max Response Length and bill at the output rate, even when the block stays collapsed. If replies come back empty or cut off, raise Max Response Length; SillyTavern's docs suggest 1024 to 4096 for reasoning models.

Errors and fixes

List the models your key can call, from the machine that runs SillyTavern:

bash

1curl https://api.relayswitch.io/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-relay-..."

  • 401: the key is wrong or revoked. Paste it again in Custom API Key and click Connect.
  • 402: the balance is too low. Top up in the console; the next message goes through.
  • 404: the model id is not in the catalog. Pick it from Available Models instead of typing it.
  • 429: the key hit its rate limit. Wait a few seconds before the next swipe.
  • A 400 naming a parameter: the model refuses that field. Add it to Exclude Body Parameters, or remove it from Include Body Parameters.
  • A 400 about roles or message order: some models want alternating user and assistant turns. Set Prompt Post-Processing in the connection panel to Semi-strict, or Strict if the first message must be the user's.
  • Connection fails or the model list stays empty: the URL is missing /v1 or ends in /chat/completions. Use https://api.relayswitch.io/v1 exactly.
  • Empty or cut-off replies: a reasoning model used up Max Response Length before it wrote the reply. Raise it.
  • Old messages forgotten: Context Size is still at 4,095. Raise it toward the model's window.

Questions

What are the best SillyTavern LLM settings?

On a hosted OpenAI-compatible API, start with Temperature 0.8 to 1.0, Top P 0.95, Frequency Penalty 0.1 to 0.3 and Presence Penalty 0 to 0.3, and set Context Size to the model's window from the Models page. Those four samplers are the ones a Custom source sends; tune them before anything else.

What does presence_penalty do in SillyTavern?

presence_penalty lowers the chance of any token that already appeared in the context, once, however often it appeared. It nudges the model toward new words and topics. frequency_penalty scales with how often a token appeared, so it targets repeated phrases. Both go to the model on a Custom source; 0 turns them off.

Do DRY settings work with an OpenAI-compatible API?

Not from the panel. DRY, XTC, Min P and Top K are Text Completion samplers, and SillyTavern does not send them for a Custom Chat Completion source. You can add a field under Additional Parameters > Include Body Parameters; the API forwards it, and whether the model applies it depends on the model.

What temperature should I use for roleplay?

Between 0.7 and 1.0 for most hosted models. Lower keeps a character consistent; higher gives more varied replies and more drift. If replies start to wander off the scene, lower temperature or Top P before adding penalties.

How much does a SillyTavern message cost?

It depends on the model and on how much history goes with each message. With 3,000 tokens in and 300 out, a message on Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $0.0045 today and on GLM 5.3 $0.0013. A larger Context Size raises the input side once the chat fills it.

What is a SillyTavern proxy?

Usually a model backend: a URL and a key that answer in the OpenAI or Anthropic format. In SillyTavern that is the Custom (OpenAI-compatible) source, or the Claude source with a Proxy Server URL. The config.yaml requestProxy setting is something else, a network proxy for SillyTavern's own traffic, and so is the reverse proxy you put in front of SillyTavern for remote access.

Is there a free SillyTavern proxy?

Not here. RelaySwitch is prepaid from $10 by card or crypto, billed per token. Before the first top-up the console chat gives 12 free turns a day to try models, in the browser, not through SillyTavern.

Does SillyTavern need the /v1 at the end?

Yes. Use https://api.relayswitch.io/v1 as the Custom Endpoint (Base URL) or Proxy Server URL. SillyTavern adds /chat/completions (or /messages on the Claude source) after it, and a URL without /v1 or with the suffix already on it fails to connect.

Can I use the Claude source with a custom URL?

Yes. Set Chat Completion Source to Claude, put https://api.relayswitch.io/v1 in Proxy Server URL and your sk-relay- key in Proxy Password. The model comes from the Claude Model dropdown, which lists fixed ids; for a Claude id it does not list, use the Custom source and type the id.
